answer:
I ran one job on IQM's free Garnet test device (garnet:mock). It held 6 circuits with 1000 shots each. The job ID is 01a160a4-2cbc-74e3-bd27-057c9b1672d7, and it completed. Mock jobs cost no credits.

What I simulated: a chain of 6 spins with the Heisenberg model, H = J sum (SxSx + SySy + SzSz), with J = 1. Every spin starts in the perfect pattern up, down, up, down, up, down. A quantum computer cannot apply this H in one step. So I cut the time into short slices of at most 0.4 and applied each neighbor interaction one slice at a time. This method is called second-order Trotter splitting. Each neighbor interaction became 3 CZ gates on the chip. The six times are 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6, and 2.0. The circuits used 0, 21, 36, 51, 66, and 81 CZ gates. I read these counts and the measured qubits back from the job the server received.

What a perfect quantum computer would show: I simulated the exact circuits the server received, with no noise. The Neel order is 1.00 at t=0, then 0.88, 0.62, 0.41, 0.34, and 0.36 at t=2.0. The exact answer of the physics model is very close at every time: 1.00, 0.88, 0.62, 0.41, 0.34, 0.37. So the time slicing adds an error of less than 0.01. The order falls fast and then levels off near 0.35. It does not drop to zero, because a chain of only 6 spins keeps some memory of where it started. It also wobbles slightly as it settles.

What the test device gave back: the Neel order came out between -0.19 and -0.41 at every time. That includes t=0, where the answer must be 1. These numbers do not track the circuit. The mock device does not run the circuit. It returns made-up bitstrings so you can check that a job is set up correctly. Each circuit got about 250 shots on each of 4 fixed patterns, such as 000000 and 111111. So the mock confirmed that the job format, the qubit choices, and the 6-circuit batch all work. It cannot show the physics. To see the melting in real data, you would run the same job on the real Garnet. Real Garnet costs credits, and its noise would add error to the deeper circuits.

What this says about KCuF3: the up-down pattern is not a stable state of the Heisenberg chain. Each pair of neighbors can swap their spins, because the model includes the SxSx + SySy terms. That swapping spreads through the chain within a time of about 1/J, and the order drops from 1 to about 0.35. In the real crystal the chains are very long, and the true lowest-energy state has no frozen up-down pattern at all. That is why KCuF3 behaves as a quantum spin liquid along its chains over a wide temperature range. Neutron scattering experiments see a broad continuum of spinon excitations rather than sharp spin waves. KCuF3 orders only below about 39 K, and only because weak couplings between neighboring chains hold the pattern in place. Even then, the ordered magnetic moment is much smaller than a full copper spin. Quantum fluctuations cause that shrinkage, and this experiment shows the same effect on a small chain.

Bit order note: the counts use IQM's raw order, with spin 1 on the left and spin 6 on the right. The Neel order gives the same value if the chain is reversed.
